title: Love Languages Quiz (Child/Teen)
description: Answered by the child/teen themselves — a forced-choice quiz where they pick which of two statements fits them better, to discover how they naturally feel loved.
instructions: For each pair, pick the statement that sounds more like you. There's no wrong answer.

scoring.method: count how many times each language letter was picked across all 30 questions; highest count = primary love language, second-highest = secondary

words.title: Words of Affirmation
words.description: You feel most loved through specific praise, encouragement, and verbal affection — hearing it said matters as much as it being true.
tips: Praise the specific effort or choice, not just "good job" — "I noticed you helped your sister without being asked" lands much harder
Say "I love you" and why fairly often — they may need to hear it more than other kids to feel secure
Be careful with harsh or joking criticism — it can land harder for this language than intended
Write small notes in a lunchbox or leave a sticky note — they'll likely keep it longer than you'd expect

time.title: Quality Time
time.description: You feel most loved through focused one-on-one attention — presence matters more than gifts or words to you.
tips: Protect small pockets of undistracted one-on-one time, even 10-15 minutes daily, over occasional big outings
Let them choose the activity sometimes — the point is your attention, not the activity itself
Put your phone away during their time — partial attention often registers to kids as no attention
Follow up later on something they told you — it shows you were really present, not just physically there

service.title: Acts of Service
service.description: You feel most loved when someone actively helps you with something — actions communicate care more than words to you.
tips: Offer to help before they have to ask twice — jumping in shows attentiveness
Let them see you doing something for them, not just doing it invisibly — narrate it briefly ("I fixed this for you")
Avoid sighing or complaining while helping — for this language, the spirit of the help matters as much as the help itself
Teach them to do things eventually, but in the moment, doing it with or for them often means more than making them do it alone

gifts.title: Receiving Gifts
gifts.description: You feel most loved through small tangible tokens — not about cost, but about being thought of.
tips: Small, frequent surprises land better than one big gift occasionally — a favorite snack or small item shows ongoing thoughtfulness
Let them keep meaningful small items rather than tidying them away — the object is tied to the memory of feeling loved
Involve them in giving gifts to others too — it reinforces the positive side of this love language
Be mindful not to substitute gifts for time or affection — pair a gift with a moment together when you can

touch.title: Physical Touch
touch.description: You feel most loved through physical affection and closeness — touch reassures you more directly than words.
tips: Build in small physical rituals — a hug before school, a specific bedtime routine — consistency matters as much as intensity
Offer physical comfort first when they're upset, before jumping to talking it through
Respect that this need may last longer than peers their age expect — that's normal, not something to discourage
A hand on the shoulder or a quick hug before something stressful (a test, a new situation) can steady them noticeably
